The fire in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area began on 8 January 1994, having originated at Cottage Point on 7 January, and spread rapidly through the adjoining Ku-ringgai Chase National Park (NSW State Coroner 1995). On 8 January, and over the next few days, wildfire burnt through bushland in the Deep Creek, Mullet Creek, Middle Creek, Jamieson Park and Wheeler Creek areas. This fire event was estimated to have burnt c. 1000 ha in the eastern section (centred on Deep Creek) of Garigal National Park (DEC NSW 2005b, 2006b). Additional bushland in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area, outside of Garigal National Park, was also burnt.

### *Field observations*

Field observations of fire responses of bushland plants were made in Lane Cove River catchment area between January 1994 and October 1999 (a period of almost 6 years), with a few occasional observations in following years (Table 3). Field observations in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area, including any flowering or fruiting of plants, were made between March 1994 and late October 1994 (over approximately 8 months). The longer period of study in the Lane Cove River area meant that more observations of postfire flowering and fruiting were made for plant species in that area, than in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment.

Observations were recorded while walking through burnt bushland after the fires. No fixed transects or quadrats were used. Observations were made along tracks, roads and walking trails throughout the study areas (Table 3). As wide a variety of habitats as possible were looked at, including bushland away from tracks and known to contain species or vegetation types that did not occur along the tracks. Most of the main tracks, and many of the minor ones, were walked at least once, and some, many times.. The total distance walked, while making observations, during the course of this study was probably in the order of several hundred kilometres. The routes walked were often the same, particularly in the more intensively studied areas. Attention was given to repeatedly observing particular species at certain locations, so that parameters such as the time of first flowering and first fruiting could be recorded for some of the rarer or more localized plant species, as well as the more common species. The author's field experience in the study areas prior to the fires was drawn upon to help locate particular species that might otherwise have been overlooked. (Some new 'discoveries' of species, previously unrecorded by the author, were made following the fires). The main references used for plant identification were Harden (1990–1993, 2002), Harden & Murray (2000), Carolin & Tindale (1994), Fairley & Moore (1989) and Robinson (1991).

In the first few months following the fires, the main focus was on whether plant species in the study areas were killed by fire or had resprouted after being burnt. Sometimes the 'skeletons' of burnt plants could be found and, if these showed no sign of resprouting for some months after the fires, then this suggested that the plants were probably killed by fire. Such skeletons occasionally retained a few scorched leaves or fruits, which helped with the identification of the species killed by the fires. Areas that had evidently experienced the highest intensity fires tended to contain far fewer identifiable plant skeletons. In these situations, the presence of woody fruits, or cones, on fatally scorched plants helped with the identification of some species. In addition, it was often possible to recall that a species had occurred at a particular site prior to that location being burnt. If such a species appeared to be absent from that same site months after the fire, or was only present in the form of post-fire seedlings, then this also helped to decide whether that species was killed in the fires. Terrestrial orchids were amongst the most difficult plants to determine, as most of them were probably seasonally dormant at the time of the fires. Presumably, the terrestrial orchids mostly sprouted from dormant subterranean tubers after the fires (as discussed by Weston *et al*. 2005).

Other data recorded, in the first few months after the fires, included the first appearance of some seedlings and the early post-fire flowering and fruiting of some plant species. As the months and years went by, the time to first flowering and fruiting was recorded for more species. The likely peaks of post-fire flowering or fruiting were also subjectively estimated for a few species. Such 'peaks' of post-fire flowering and fruiting may plateau over a number of years. These estimates are probably best regarded as broadly indicative as their estimation may have been affected by the subjective nature of the observations and by variability between and within populations. The rate of maturation tends to vary between individual plants, within any population of a given species (e.g. see Benson 1985).

### *Fire patchiness and intensity*

Benson (1985) suggested that varying fire intensities within single fire events are a common feature of fires affecting Hawkesbury sandstone vegetation in the Sydney region, and indicated that such variability may be, at least in part, due to landscape or habitat variation. Keith *et al*. (2002a) noted that topographically varied areas, such as the sandstone plateaus of the Sydney region, are likely to exhibit greater fire patchiness than areas of heathland burnt on extensive plains. Walsh & McDougall (2004) also reported variability in the wildfire intensity in the treeless subalpine vegetation of Kosciuszko National Park in southern NSW. Patches of vegetation that have not been burnt by a particular fire can act as fire 'refuges'. Such fire refuges can protect fire sensitive species and also provide sources of seed for dispersal to burnt areas after fires (Benson 1985, Williams *et al*. 1994, Gill & Bradstock 1995, Bradstock *et al*. 1997, Whelan *et al*. 2002). Morrison (2002) studied the effects of fire intensity on the plant species composition of bushland in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, following a wildfire of early January 1994.

# **Results and discussion**

Fire responses for 828 vascular plant species (576 native and 252 exotic species) were recorded in bushland of the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon catchments, following the wildfires of January 1994 (Appendix 1). In many cases it was possible to determine whether a species resprouted or was killed by the fires, and generally, the more widespread and common a species, the greater was the opportunity to reliably determine the mode of regeneration. All fire responses reported here are for individual plants whose above-ground parts were 100% scorched. The responses of individual plants that were only partly burnt are not included.

It was not practicable to record data in all of the categories for all of the 828 species of plants because of the logistical challenges for one observer recording information across large areas of bushland, over a number of years. The first post-fire flowering, or fruiting, of some of the locally rarer species may have been missed. For example, the orchid *Orthoceras strictum* is rare in the bushland of the Lane Cove River area and one plant was seen with green fruits in January 1996, but it is possible that this species may have flowered a year earlier and simply been overlooked, due to its local rarity and inconspicuous colouration.

### *Fire responses of ferns and fern allies*

The ferns and fern allies (pteridophytes) mostly resprouted after the January 1994 wildfires. The exceptions were mostly epiphytic or lithophytic species, such as *Hymenophyllum cupressiforme* (Hymenophyllaceae) and *Pyrrosia rupestris*  (Polypodiaceae), which were killed when severely scorched. Most of the resprouting pteridophytes regenerated from below the ground, presumably from buried rhizomes. The treefern *Cyathea australis* (Cyatheaceae) resprouted from the apex of the trunk after the fires. Benson & McDougall (1993) noted that old plants may survive many bushfires. *Calochlaena dubia* (Dicksoniaceae) and *Pteridium esculentum* (Dennstaedtiaceae) resprouted very vigorously but a few *Calochlaena dubia* rhizomes were apparently killed by fire, probably because they were growing in shallow soil on top of a boulder. Benson & McDougall (1993) stated that *Calochlaena dubia* is a vigorous resprouter following fire and may produce shoots within a month of burning, even in the absence of rain.

The majority of the resprouting ferns produced spores within the first year after the fires. Amongst the earliest resprouting ferns to produce spores were *Blechnum cartilagineum*  (Blechnaceae), *Pteridium esculentum* (Dennstaedtiaceae) and *Todea barbara* (Osmundaceae). These species had some fronds with mature sporangia by 10 weeks (March 1994) after the fires. L. McDougall observed that vigorous regrowth of *Blechnum cartilagineum* produced fertile fronds in less than 20 weeks after a high intensity fire at Killarney Heights, in northern Sydney (Benson & McDougall 1993).

### *Fire responses of conifers*

Bond & van Wilgen (1996) stated that resprouting after fire is much rarer in conifers than in woody angiosperms. Of the few species of conifer in the study area *Callitris muelleri*  (Cupressaceae) was killed by fire in the Narrabeen Lagoon area. At one site, seedlings (2 – 6 cm tall) were observed growing in the vicinity of fatally scorched adult plants, within 32 weeks of burning, and evidently grew from seed that was shed from cones, which opened after the fire, on the standing plants. Benson & McDougall (1993) recorded that this species is killed by fire and that seedling recruitment occurs mainly after fire.

Benson & McDougall (1993) documented that the low-growing coniferous shrub *Podocarpus spinulosus*  (Podocarpaceae) resprouts at ground level or below, after being burnt and noted that this species probably has no soilstored seedbank and that its seed is probably dispersed by birds. *Podocarpus spinulosus* resprouted vigorously after the 1994 fires in the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon areas – no seedlings were observed in the burnt bushland of the Lane Cove River area in the first few years after the January 1994 fires. The resprouted male and female plants in the Lane Cove River area first started flowering in October 1995 and some mature fruit were produced by early December 1995 (c. 100 weeks after the fires). Stems of male plants occurred in groups separate from the grouped stems of female plants probably indicating spread by vegetative means.

Field observations of fire responses of bushland plants were made in Lane Cove River catchment area between January 1994 and October 1999 (a period of almost 6 years), with a few occasional observations in following years (Table 3). Field observations in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area, including any flowering or fruiting of plants, were made between March 1994 and late October 1994 (over approximately 8 months). The longer period of study in the Lane Cove River area meant that more observations of postfire flowering and fruiting were made for plant species in that area, than in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment.

Observations were recorded while walking through burnt bushland after the fires. No fixed transects or quadrats were used. Observations were made along tracks, roads and walking trails throughout the study areas (Table 3). As wide a variety of habitats as possible were looked at, including bushland away from tracks and known to contain species or vegetation types that did not occur along the tracks. Most of the main tracks, and many of the minor ones, were walked at least once, and some, many times.. The total distance walked, while making observations, during the course of this study was probably in the order of several hundred kilometres. The routes walked were often the same, particularly in the more intensively studied areas. Attention was given to repeatedly observing particular species at certain locations, so that parameters such as the time of first flowering and first fruiting could be recorded for some of the rarer or more localized plant species, as well as the more common species. The author's field experience in the study areas prior to the fires was drawn upon to help locate particular species that might otherwise have been overlooked. (Some new 'discoveries' of species, previously unrecorded by the author, were made following the fires). The main references used for plant identification were Harden (1990–1993, 2002), Harden & Murray (2000), Carolin & Tindale (1994), Fairley & Moore (1989) and Robinson (1991).

In the first few months following the fires, the main focus was on whether plant species in the study areas were killed by fire or had resprouted after being burnt. Sometimes the 'skeletons' of burnt plants could be found and, if these showed no sign of resprouting for some months after the fires, then this suggested that the plants were probably killed by fire. Such skeletons occasionally retained a few scorched leaves or fruits, which helped with the identification of the species killed by the fires. Areas that had evidently experienced the highest intensity fires tended to contain far fewer identifiable plant skeletons. In these situations, the presence of woody fruits, or cones, on fatally scorched plants helped with the identification of some species. In addition, it was often possible to recall that a species had occurred at a particular site prior to that location being burnt. If such a species appeared to be absent from that same site months after the fire, or was only present in the form of post-fire seedlings, then this also helped to decide whether that species was killed in the fires. Terrestrial orchids were amongst the most difficult plants to determine, as most of them were probably seasonally dormant at the time of the fires. Presumably, the terrestrial orchids mostly sprouted from dormant subterranean tubers after the fires (as discussed by Weston *et al*. 2005).

Other data recorded, in the first few months after the fires, included the first appearance of some seedlings and the early post-fire flowering and fruiting of some plant species. As the months and years went by, the time to first flowering and fruiting was recorded for more species. The likely peaks of post-fire flowering or fruiting were also subjectively estimated for a few species. Such 'peaks' of post-fire flowering and fruiting may plateau over a number of years. These estimates are probably best regarded as broadly indicative as their estimation may have been affected by the subjective nature of the observations and by variability between and within populations. The rate of maturation tends to vary between individual plants, within any population of a given species (e.g. see Benson 1985).

### *Fire patchiness and intensity*

Benson (1985) suggested that varying fire intensities within single fire events are a common feature of fires affecting Hawkesbury sandstone vegetation in the Sydney region, and indicated that such variability may be, at least in part, due to landscape or habitat variation. Keith *et al*. (2002a) noted that topographically varied areas, such as the sandstone plateaus of the Sydney region, are likely to exhibit greater fire patchiness than areas of heathland burnt on extensive plains. Walsh & McDougall (2004) also reported variability in the wildfire intensity in the treeless subalpine vegetation of Kosciuszko National Park in southern NSW. Patches of vegetation that have not been burnt by a particular fire can act as fire 'refuges'. Such fire refuges can protect fire sensitive species and also provide sources of seed for dispersal to burnt areas after fires (Benson 1985, Williams *et al*. 1994, Gill & Bradstock 1995, Bradstock *et al*. 1997, Whelan *et al*. 2002). Morrison (2002) studied the effects of fire intensity on the plant species composition of bushland in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, following a wildfire of early January 1994.

The January 1994 fires in the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon areas were generally of an apparently high intensity

Observations of plant responses in apparently lower fire intensities were used to help understand the responses of the same species in the more severely scorched areas. For example, if a species was observed as being killed (as evidenced by the presence of scorched, dead plant skeletons) in the lower intensity areas (e.g. some of the edges of burnt areas), then this information complemented any observations that no plants of the same species could be found resprouting in the immediately adjoining areas that were evidently burnt at a higher intensity.

# **Results and discussion**

Fire responses for 828 vascular plant species (576 native and 252 exotic species) were recorded in bushland of the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon catchments, following the wildfires of January 1994 (Appendix 1). In many cases it was possible to determine whether a species resprouted or was killed by the fires, and generally, the more widespread and common a species, the greater was the opportunity to reliably determine the mode of regeneration. All fire responses reported here are for individual plants whose above-ground parts were 100% scorched. The responses of individual plants that were only partly burnt are not included.

It was not practicable to record data in all of the categories for all of the 828 species of plants because of the logistical challenges for one observer recording information across large areas of bushland, over a number of years. The first post-fire flowering, or fruiting, of some of the locally rarer species may have been missed. For example, the orchid *Orthoceras strictum* is rare in the bushland of the Lane Cove River area and one plant was seen with green fruits in January 1996, but it is possible that this species may have flowered a year earlier and simply been overlooked, due to its local rarity and inconspicuous colouration.

### *Fire responses of ferns and fern allies*

The ferns and fern allies (pteridophytes) mostly resprouted after the January 1994 wildfires. The exceptions were mostly epiphytic or lithophytic species, such as *Hymenophyllum cupressiforme* (Hymenophyllaceae) and *Pyrrosia rupestris*  (Polypodiaceae), which were killed when severely scorched. Most of the resprouting pteridophytes regenerated from below the ground, presumably from buried rhizomes. The treefern *Cyathea australis* (Cyatheaceae) resprouted from the apex of the trunk after the fires. Benson & McDougall (1993) noted that old plants may survive many bushfires. *Calochlaena dubia* (Dicksoniaceae) and *Pteridium esculentum* (Dennstaedtiaceae) resprouted very vigorously but a few *Calochlaena dubia* rhizomes were apparently killed by fire, probably because they were growing in shallow soil on top of a boulder. Benson & McDougall (1993) stated that *Calochlaena dubia* is a vigorous resprouter following fire and may produce shoots within a month of burning, even in the absence of rain.

The majority of the resprouting ferns produced spores within the first year after the fires. Amongst the earliest resprouting ferns to produce spores were *Blechnum cartilagineum*  (Blechnaceae), *Pteridium esculentum* (Dennstaedtiaceae) and *Todea barbara* (Osmundaceae). These species had some fronds with mature sporangia by 10 weeks (March 1994) after the fires. L. McDougall observed that vigorous regrowth of *Blechnum cartilagineum* produced fertile fronds in less than 20 weeks after a high intensity fire at Killarney Heights, in northern Sydney (Benson & McDougall 1993).

### *Fire responses of conifers*

Bond & van Wilgen (1996) stated that resprouting after fire is much rarer in conifers than in woody angiosperms. Of the few species of conifer in the study area *Callitris muelleri*  (Cupressaceae) was killed by fire in the Narrabeen Lagoon area. At one site, seedlings (2 – 6 cm tall) were observed growing in the vicinity of fatally scorched adult plants, within 32 weeks of burning, and evidently grew from seed that was shed from cones, which opened after the fire, on the standing plants. Benson & McDougall (1993) recorded that this species is killed by fire and that seedling recruitment occurs mainly after fire.

Benson & McDougall (1993) documented that the low-growing coniferous shrub *Podocarpus spinulosus*  (Podocarpaceae) resprouts at ground level or below, after being burnt and noted that this species probably has no soilstored seedbank and that its seed is probably dispersed by birds. *Podocarpus spinulosus* resprouted vigorously after the 1994 fires in the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon areas – no seedlings were observed in the burnt bushland of the Lane Cove River area in the first few years after the January 1994 fires. The resprouted male and female plants in the Lane Cove River area first started flowering in October 1995 and some mature fruit were produced by early December 1995 (c. 100 weeks after the fires). Stems of male plants occurred in groups separate from the grouped stems of female plants probably indicating spread by vegetative means.

### *Fire responses of monocotyledons*

The great majority of monocotyledons resprouted following the 1994 fires, but a few species were killed e.g. *Caustis flexuosa* and *Caustis pentandra* (Cyperaceae). D. Benson

import csv, re, sys, random, json

PAPER = "data/papers_test/md_llm/Kubiak_2009.md"
OUT = sys.argv[1]
text = open(PAPER).read()
pages = text.split("<!-- PAGE BREAK -->")
COLUMNS = list(csv.reader(open("data/inference_test/results/sonnet-5-5_raw.csv")))[0]
assert len(COLUMNS) == 39

def sent(key, n=None):
    i = text.find(key)
    j = text.find(". ", i) + 1
    s = text[i:j]
    assert s and "\n" not in s, key
    return s

Q_ABS = sent("In early January 1994 wildfires")
Q_LCR = sent("The Lane Cove River valley is situated")
Q_NL = sent("The Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area is about")
Q_FIRE_LCR = sent("The Lane Cove River fire began")
Q_FIRE_NL = sent("The fire in the Narrabeen Lagoon catchment area began")
Q_SEV = "The January 1994 fires in the Lane Cove River and Narrabeen Lagoon areas were generally of an apparently high intensity"
Q_SCORCH = sent("All fire responses reported here")
assert Q_SEV in text

SOURCE = "kubiak, p. j. (2009). fire responses of bushland plants after the january 1994 wildfires in northern sydney. cunninghamia, 11(1), 131-165."
PAPERWIDE = ("fire responses are for individual plants whose above-ground parts were 100% scorched (p. 136); "
             "first flowering and fruiting times are weeks (w) or years (y) after the january 1994 fires; "
             "c. = approximately, (1) = one plant, (shd) = shedding seed or spores, grn = green fruit, imm = immature fruit, ri = ripe fruit, "
             "adv = advanced seedlings, m.i.f = moderate intensity fire, buds = flowers in bud (p. 145); "
             "bold flowering time = sizable proportion of population flowering; underlined time in both resp and seed columns = unclear whether plants grew from seed or resprouted (p. 145); "
             "observations in lane cove river mainly jan 1994-oct 1999 and in narrabeen lagoon mar-oct 1994 (p. 145); "
             "flowering and juvenile period times are printed once per species, not split by site")

DEF = {
    "R": "majority of adult plants resprouted after the fires",
    "K": "majority of adult plants killed by the fires",
    "r": "a small proportion of adult plants of this species resprouted after the fires",
    "k": "a small proportion of adult plants of this species were killed by the fires",
    "pR": "probably resprouted after the fires", "pK": "probably killed by the fires",
    "?R": "possibly resprouted", "?K": "possibly killed",
}
CERT = {"p": "'probably' = say 80-90% sure of observation", "?": "'possibly' = say 50-70% sure of observation"}

def fire_response(code):
    """-> (value, note)"""
    c = code.replace(" ", "")
    simple = {"R": "resprouter", "K": "obligate"}
    if c in simple:
        return simple[c], ""
    if c in ("pR", "?R", "pK", "?K"):
        v = "resprouter" if c.endswith("R") else "obligate"
        return v, f"fire response code printed '{c}' = {DEF[c]}; certainty as stated in the paper: {CERT[c[0]]}"
    if c == "K/r":
        return "O/r", f"fire response code printed 'K/r' = K: {DEF['K']}; r: {DEF['r']}"
    if c == "R/k":
        return "R/o", f"fire response code printed 'R/k' = R: {DEF['R']}; k: {DEF['k']}"
    if c == "pK/r":
        return "O/r", f"fire response code printed 'pK/r' = pK: {DEF['pK']}; r: {DEF['r']}; certainty as stated in the paper: {CERT['p']}"
    if c == "?K/r":
        return "O/r", f"fire response code printed '?K/r' = ?K: {DEF['?K']}; r: {DEF['r']}; certainty as stated in the paper: {CERT['?']}"
    if c == "R/?k":
        return "R/o", f"fire response code printed 'R/?k' = R: {DEF['R']}; ?k: possibly a small proportion killed; certainty as stated in the paper: {CERT['?']}"
    if c in ("K/R", "R/K"):
        a, b = c.split("/")
        return "", f"fire response codes printed '{a}' = {DEF[a]}; '{b}' = {DEF[b]}; conflicting codes"
    if c in ("k/r",):
        return "", f"fire response codes printed 'k' = {DEF['k']}; 'r' = {DEF['r']}; no clear class"
    if c in ("k", "r"):
        return "", f"fire response code printed '{c}' = {DEF[c]}; no clear class"
    if c in ("?k", "?r"):
        return "", f"fire response code printed '{c}' = possibly {DEF[c[1]]}; no clear class; certainty as stated in the paper: {CERT['?']}"
    if c.startswith("K;r"):
        return "", f"fire response cell printed '{code}': 'K' = {DEF['K']}; 'r' = {DEF['r']}; conflicting codes (m.i.f = moderate intensity fire)"
    if c.startswith("R(1)m.i.f"):
        return "", f"fire response cell printed '{code}': R = {DEF['R']}; no clear class, the paper states the host canopy was not 100% scorched"
    raise ValueError(code)

CODE_RE = re.compile(r"^(\?|p)?[RKrk](/\??[RKrk])?$|^K;r.*$|^R\(1\)m\.i\.f.*$|^\? r$")

# ---------- time parsing ----------
UNIT = {"w": "weeks", "y": "years"}
TIME_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:c\.\s*)?\??\s*(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)(?:\s*[\u2013-]\s*(\d+(?:\.\d+)?))?(\+)?\s*(w|y)")

def clean(cell):
    return cell.replace("<u>", "").replace("</u>", "").replace("**", "").strip()

def parse_time(cell):
    """-> value string '<v> <unit>' or None"""
    s = clean(cell)
    if not s:
        return None
    if s == "At least 5 years":
        return ">5 years"
    if s == "Less than 1 year":
        return "<1 years"
    m = TIME_RE.match(s)
    if m:
        a, b, plus, u = m.groups()
        v = a + ("-" + b if b else "")
        if plus:
            v = ">" + v
        return f"{v} {UNIT[u]}"
    m = re.match(r"^(\d+),", s)
    if m:
        u = re.search(r"(w|y)\b", s)
        if u:
            return f"{m.group(1)} {UNIT[u.group(1)]}"
    return None

# ---------- names ----------
def parse_name(raw):
    notes = []
    s = raw.strip()
    exotic = False
    if s.startswith("(*?)"):
        s = s[4:]
        notes.append("native_status left empty: name printed with '(*?)'")
    elif s.startswith("*"):
        exotic = True
        s = s[1:]
    peak = ""
    m = re.search(r"\s*\(((?:poss|prob)\.pk\.pf\.[^)]*)\)\s*$", s)
    if m:
        peak = m.group(1)
        s = s[:m.start()]
        kind = "possible" if peak.startswith("poss") else "probable"
        what = "fruiting" if "fruit" in peak else "flowering"
        notes.append(f"species printed with '({peak})' = {kind} peak of post-fire {what} in the left hand column")
    for pat, lab in ((r"\s*\((s\.(?:lat|str)\.)\)", None), (r"\s*\((syn\. [^)]*)\)", None)):
        m = re.search(pat, s)
        if m:
            notes.append(f"species name printed with '({m.group(1)})'")
            s = s[:m.start()] + s[m.end():]
    printed = s
    toks = s.replace("\u201c", "").replace("\u201d", "").split()
    genus = toks[0]
    rest = toks[1:]
    subsp = ""
    species = ""
    i = 0
    if rest and rest[0] in ("x", "X"):
        rest = rest[1:]
    if rest and rest[0].startswith("species"):
        species = " ".join(rest)
        rest = []
    elif rest:
        species = rest[0].strip("?").replace("\u2013", "-").strip("()")
        rest = rest[1:]
    if rest:
        rank = rest[0]
        nm = " ".join(rest[1:]).strip("?").replace("\u2013", "-")
        subsp = f"{rank} {nm}"
    genus = genus.replace("\u2013", "-")
    composed = f"{genus} {species}" + (f" {subsp}" if subsp else "")
    if composed != printed:
        notes.append(f"name printed as '{printed}'")
    return dict(genus=genus, species=species, subsp=subsp, exotic=exotic, notes=notes)

# ---------- read table ----------
rows = []
family = None
for pi in range(14, 35):
    header = None
    for l in pages[pi].split("\n"):
        if not l.startswith("|") or l.startswith("|---"):
            continue
        c = [x.strip() for x in l.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
        if c[0].startswith("Family/"):
            header = l
            continue
        assert len(c) == 10, l
        if c[0].startswith("**") and all(x == "" for x in c[1:]):
            name = c[0].strip("*")
            if name in ("PTERIDOPHYTES", "GYMNOSPERMS", "DICOTYLEDONS", "MONOCOTYLEDONS"):
                continue
            family = (name.lower(), l, pi + 1)
            continue
        rows.append(dict(cells=c, line=l, page=pi + 1, header=header, family=family))
print("species rows", len(rows), file=sys.stderr)

def norm(l):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", l).strip()

SITES = {
    "lcr": dict(name="lane cove river valley", lat="-33.75", lon="151.0833"),
    "nl": dict(name="narrabeen lagoon catchment area", lat="-33.75", lon="151.0833"),
}

def fire_cols(site):
    """site: 'lcr', 'nl' or 'both' -> dict of fill + data_location/quote parts + notes"""
    d = dict(fire_type="wildfire", fire_season_categorical="summer", fire_severity_categorical="high")
    loc, quo, notes = [], [], []
    if site == "lcr":
        loc += ["site: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_LCR]
        loc += ["fire type: abstract, p. 131"]; quo += [Q_ABS]
        loc += ["fire season: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_FIRE_LCR]
        notes += ["fire_season_categorical derived from fire date 6 january 1994"]
        d.update(location_name=SITES["lcr"]["name"], latitude="-33.75", longitude="151.0833")

             "first flowering and fruiting times are weeks (w) or years (y) after the january 1994 fires; "
             "c. = approximately, (1) = one plant, (shd) = shedding seed or spores, grn = green fruit, imm = immature fruit, ri = ripe fruit, "
             "adv = advanced seedlings, m.i.f = moderate intensity fire, buds = flowers in bud (p. 145); "
             "bold flowering time = sizable proportion of population flowering; underlined time in both resp and seed columns = unclear whether plants grew from seed or resprouted (p. 145); "
             "observations in lane cove river mainly jan 1994-oct 1999 and in narrabeen lagoon mar-oct 1994 (p. 145); "
             "flowering and juvenile period times are printed once per species, not split by site")

DEF = {
    "R": "majority of adult plants resprouted after the fires",
    "K": "majority of adult plants killed by the fires",
    "r": "a small proportion of adult plants of this species resprouted after the fires",
    "k": "a small proportion of adult plants of this species were killed by the fires",
    "pR": "probably resprouted after the fires", "pK": "probably killed by the fires",

}

    composed = f"{genus} {species}" + (f" {subsp}" if subsp else "")
    if composed != printed:
        notes.append(f"name printed as '{printed}'")
    return dict(genus=genus, species=species, subsp=subsp, exotic=exotic, notes=notes)

# ---------- read table ----------
rows = []
family = None
for pi in range(14, 35):
    header = None
    for l in pages[pi].split("\n"):
        if not l.startswith("|") or l.startswith("|---"):
            continue
        c = [x.strip() for x in l.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
        if c[0].startswith("Family/"):
            header = l
            continue
        assert len(c) == 10, l
        if c[0].startswith("**") and all(x == "" for x in c[1:]):
            name = c[0].strip("*")
            if name in ("PTERIDOPHYTES", "GYMNOSPERMS", "DICOTYLEDONS", "MONOCOTYLEDONS"):
                continue
            family = (name.lower(), l, pi + 1)
            continue
        rows.append(dict(cells=c, line=l, page=pi + 1, header=header, family=family))
print("species rows", len(rows), file=sys.stderr)

def norm(l):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", l).strip()

SITES = {
    "lcr": dict(name="lane cove river valley", lat="-33.75", lon="151.0833"),
    "nl": dict(name="narrabeen lagoon catchment area", lat="-33.75", lon="151.0833"),
}

def fire_cols(site):
    """site: 'lcr', 'nl' or 'both' -> dict of fill + data_location/quote parts + notes"""
    d = dict(fire_type="wildfire", fire_season_categorical="summer", fire_severity_categorical="high")
    loc, quo, notes = [], [], []
    if site == "lcr":
        loc += ["site: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_LCR]
        loc += ["fire type: abstract, p. 131"]; quo += [Q_ABS]
        loc += ["fire season: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_FIRE_LCR]
        notes += ["fire_season_categorical derived from fire date 6 january 1994"]
        d.update(location_name=SITES["lcr"]["name"], latitude="-33.75", longitude="151.0833")
    elif site == "nl":
        loc += ["site: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_NL]
        loc += ["coordinates and fire type: abstract, p. 131"]; quo += [Q_ABS]
        loc += ["fire season: methods, p. 134"]; quo += [Q_FIRE_NL]
        notes += ["fire_season_categorical derived from fire date 8 january 1994",
                  "coordinates printed once for the northern sydney study area (abstract)"]
        d.update(location_name=SITES["nl"]["name"], latitude="-33.75", longitude="151.0833")
    else:
        loc += ["site: methods, p. 133"]; quo += [Q_LCR + " ... " + Q_NL]
        loc += ["fire type: abstract, p. 131"]; quo += [Q_ABS]
        loc += ["fire season: methods, p. 133", "fire season: methods, p. 134"]; quo += [Q_FIRE_LCR, Q_FIRE_NL]
        notes += ["fire_season_categorical derived from fire dates 6 january 1994 (lane cove river) and 8 january 1994 (narrabeen lagoon)"]
        d.update(location_name=SITES["lcr"]["name"] + "; " + SITES["nl"]["name"])
    loc += ["fire severity: methods, p. 134"]; quo += [Q_SEV]
    notes += ["fire_severity_categorical printed 'apparently high intensity'"]
    return d, loc, quo, notes

def build():
    out = []
    stats = dict(rows=0, species=0, no_row=[])
    for r in rows:
        c = r["cells"]
        nm = parse_name(c[0])
        stats["species"] += 1
        lcr_cell, nl_cell = c[1], c[2]
        sites = []
        extra_notes = []
        resp = {}
        for key, cell, lab in (("lcr", lcr_cell, "lane cove river"), ("nl", nl_cell, "narrabeen lagoon")):
            if cell and CODE_RE.match(cell):
                resp[key] = fire_response(cell)
                sites.append(key)
            elif cell:
                extra_notes.append(f"{lab} fire response cell printed '{cell}'")
        # time columns
        fill = {}
        tnotes = []
        cols = {4: "time_to_first_flower_production_resprout_repr3a", 5: "age_at_first_flower_production_from_seed_repr3",
                8: "primary_juvenile_period", 9: "secondary_juvenile_period"}
        under = {}
        for i, col in cols.items():
            cell = c[i]
            if not cell:
                continue
            if i in (4, 5) and "<u>" in cell:
                under[i] = cell
                continue
            v = parse_time(cell)
            if v is None:
                tnotes.append(f"{col} not filled, cell printed '{clean(cell)}'")
                continue
            fill[col] = v
            if not re.fullmatch(r"\d+w", cell):
                tnotes.append(f"{col} printed '{clean(cell)}'" if "**" not in cell else f"{col} printed '{cell}'")
        if under:
            cs = sorted(set(clean(x) for x in under.values()))
            labs = "resp and seed columns" if len(under) == 2 else ("resp column" if 4 in under else "seed column")
            tnotes.append(f"first flowering underlined in {labs}, printed '{'; '.join(cs)}', unclear whether plants grew from seed or resprouted")
        fr = [(c[6], c[7])]
        if c[6] or c[7]:
            if c[6] and c[7] and clean(c[6]) == clean(c[7]) and "<u>" in c[6]:
                tnotes.append(f"first fruiting underlined in resp and seed columns, printed '{clean(c[6])}', unclear whether plants grew from seed or resprouted")
            else:
                if c[6]:
                    tnotes.append(f"first fruiting (resprouted plants) printed '{clean(c[6])}'" + (" underlined" if "<u>" in c[6] else ""))
                if c[7]:
                    tnotes.append(f"first fruiting (plants from seed) printed '{clean(c[7])}'" + (" underlined" if "<u>" in c[7] else ""))
        if c[3]:
            tnotes.append(f"seedlings first observed printed '{clean(c[3])}'")
        # peaks etc
        base = list(nm["notes"])
        hasfill = bool(fill)
        specs = []  # (site, resp, timefill)
        if len(sites) == 2:
            for s in sites:
                specs.append((s, resp[s], {}))
            if hasfill:
                specs.append(("both", ("", ""), fill))
        elif len(sites) == 1:
            specs.append((sites[0], resp[sites[0]], fill))
        else:
            if hasfill:
                specs.append(("both", ("", ""), fill))
        if not specs:
            stats["no_row"].append(c[0])
            continue
        shared_row = any(s == "both" for s, _, _ in specs)
        for site, (frv, frn), tf in specs:
            row = {k: "" for k in COLUMNS}
            row.update(genus=nm["genus"], species=nm["species"], subsp=nm["subsp"])
            if nm["exotic"]:
                row["native_status"] = "exotic"
            fam = r["family"]
            row["family"] = fam[0] if fam else ""
            row["fire_response_categorical_surv1"] = frv
            row.update(tf)
            fd, floc, fquo, fnotes = fire_cols(site)
            row.update(fd)
            # notes
            n1 = []
            if frn:
                n1.append(frn)
            n1 += base
            n1 += extra_notes
            if site == "both":
                n1.append("value printed once for the species in appendix 1, not split by site, recorded at both sites or site not stated; coordinates left empty")
                if not sites:
                    n1.append("species has no fire response code in either site column")
            if (site != "both") or True:
                if site == "both" or not shared_row:
                    n1 += tnotes
            n1 += fnotes
            row["notes"] = "; ".join(n1 + [PAPERWIDE])
            row["source"] = SOURCE
            row["file_name"] = "Kubiak_2009"
            row["supplementary_material"] = ""
            # data location/quote
            p = r["page"] + 130
            qrow = norm(r["line"])
            famline = norm(fam[1]) if fam else ""
            hdr = norm(r["header"]) if r["header"] else ""
            what = "fire response and times" if (frv or site != "both") and site != "both" else "times"
            if site != "both" and not tf:
                what = "fire response"
            loc = []
            quo = []
            if fam and fam[2] == r["page"]:
                loc.append(f"{what}: appendix 1, p. {p}")
                quo.append(" ... ".join([qrow, famline, hdr]))
            else:
                loc.append(f"{what}: appendix 1, p. {p}")
                quo.append(" ... ".join([qrow, hdr]))
                if fam:
                    loc.append(f"family: appendix 1, p. {fam[2] + 130}")
                    quo.append(famline)
            loc += floc
            quo += fquo
            row["data_location"] = "; ".join(loc)
            row["data_quote"] = "; ".join(f"[{a}] {b}" for a, b in zip(loc, quo))
            out.append(row)
    return out, stats

out, stats = build()
print("rows", len(out), "species", stats["species"], "no_row", len(stats["no_row"]), file=sys.stderr)
print("no_row sample", stats["no_row"][:40], file=sys.stderr)
with open(OUT, "w", newline="") as f:

import csv, re, sys
PAPER = "data/papers_test/md_llm/NSWNPWS_2004.md"
OUT = sys.argv[1]
t = open(PAPER).read().split("<!-- PAGE BREAK -->")
COLUMNS = list(csv.reader(open("data/inference_test/results/sonnet-5-5_raw.csv")))[0]

def norm(l):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", l).strip()

def tab(p):
    hdr, out = None, []
    for l in p.split("\n"):
        if l.startswith("|") and not l.startswith("|---"):
            c = [x.strip() for x in l.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
            if c[0] == "Species":
                hdr = norm(l)
                continue

Aust. J. Bot., 1989, 37, 1-18

# Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by *Acacia verticillata* (L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

## Abstract

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

## Introduction

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. On the upper slopes, shrubs of *Kunzea ambigua* had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, *Melaleuca ericifolia*, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

## Materials and Methods

### Vegetation Structure and Composition

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

### Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub

An experimental plot 200 m² was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

# Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by *Acacia verticillata* (L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

## Abstract

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

## Introduction

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. ## Materials and Methods

### Vegetation Structure and Composition

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

### Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub

An experimental plot 200 m² was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. # Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats

## Tony D. Auld and Judith Scott

*New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville N.S.W. 2220, Australia*
*Tel. +61 02 9585 6497; Fax +61 02 9585 6495; E-mail tauld@pws.nsw.gov.au*

**Abstract.** A number of endangered plant species occur in National Parks and associated bushland that are adjacent to urban areas in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia. Within these areas fire is a repeated and frequent disturbance event that potentially threatens not only the endangered flora but life and property as well. These threats were well illustrated by the impact of the fires that occurred in January 1994 in Sydney.
For the management of such fire-prone areas there is a need to identify those fire regimes likely to drive the endangered flora to extinction. Management of fire-sensitive, threatened *Darwinia* (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* (Proteaceae) species illustrates how conservation goals can be applied along with protection of life and property. A regime of frequent fire will lead to local population declines and extinction in both *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species. Consequently, frequent burning on a regular basis for hazard reduction to protect property assets is inappropriate for the conservation of these species. *Darwinia* species also require fires that cause significant soil heating (high consumption of fine fuel) to break seed dormancy in soil stored seed, while *Grevillea* species require fires of a large spatial extent to minimise the impact of mammalian seed predators on seed outputs from the first few seed-crops produced by plants after a fire.

**Keywords:** Fire regime; Threatened species; *Darwinia*; *Grevillea*

## Introduction

In the Sydney Region of southeastern Australia, much of the vegetation is highly flammable and fires are a common and frequent event. For example, during January of 1994, some 90% and 65% respectively of the two major, large urban reserves (Royal and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Parks) were burnt. In this rich and diverse floristic area, around 2000 plant species regularly experience fire. As a consequence, the management of fire is one of the principal challenges facing managers of natural ecosystems in the Sydney Region. Managers must attempt to protect life and property from the dangers posed by fire in urban bushland as well as conserving this biodiversity.

Given the high potential for extreme fire events, where effective control of wildfire is not always possible (as happened in January 1994), there is increasing pressure for widespread fuel reduction burning in urban bushland adjacent to human assets such as houses. Such areas contain a number of endangered, vulnerable or rare plant species that are of high conservation significance, as well as more common species, all of which will have particular fire requirements which may or may not be compatible with burning for fuel reduction purposes. Hence, there is a potential for a conflict over protection versus conservation priorities (Bradstock, Keith & Auld 1995, Bradstock & Scott 1995). To attempt to resolve such conflicts we must have a sound knowledge of the effects of different fire regimes on plant and animal species and as land managers apply an informed choice of appropriate fire regimes to ensure the maintenance of populations of plants and animals.

This paper presents data on the effect of different components of the fire regime on several threatened plant species in order to provide land managers with potential conservation prescriptions for threatened plant species. In particular, we identify those fire regimes that may cause populations to decline. Such prescriptions can then be incorporated into planning and the implementation of a fuel reduction program, so that conservation issues are not ignored and fire regimes which threaten plant conservation are avoided.

## Study Area

The Sydney area in south-eastern Australia is a large urban area fringed with large bushland reserves and containing many smaller reserves (Figure 1). Within this area, the vegetation is dominated by sclerophyll heathlands, woodlands and forests, situated on infertile sandy soils derived from Hawkesbury sandstone (Beadle 1981), in a landscape of dissected sandstone plateaux. Rainfall is around 1200mm per annum with a peak in late summer. Average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures for

Sydney are 26/18°C in summer and 16/8°C in winter. A broad range of fire regimes are possible in the Sydney Region. High intensity wildfires occur in the order of once every 5-10 years, while deliberate prescriptions of low intensity fires are commonly used for fuel reduction. Arson is a major source of wildfire ignitions.

## The Fire Regime

For the long term survival of plants and animals we need to know how they are affected by the fire regime, ie. (frequency, intensity, season, spatial extent). Here we concentrate on fire-sensitive plants.

### *Fire frequency*

All fires burn areas of vegetation that have been burnt some time before. Consequently, the vegetation is really a mosaic of fire histories, with some parts having had more fires than others over a given time period. We need to try and understand how important this unequal patchiness of fires through time is for the survival of plants.

Plants that are killed by fire rely on seed germination after fires to survive at a particular location. For these fire-sensitive plants, there must be sufficient time between successive fires for seedlings to mature and produce more seeds and hence, add seeds to the seedbank. In the Sydney area, this time will vary between species and loca-


<<PB>>


- Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats - 165

tions (Benson 1985), from species that flower within 1-2 years after fire (*Actinotus helianthi*, *Acacia suaveolens*) to those that may take 4-8 years to reach maturity (*Banksia ericifolia*). If another fire should occur before these plants have matured, dramatic changes in the vegetation may occur. Fire-sensitive plants with seed stored in woody capsules usually release all their seeds after a fire and no residual seeds remain in cones. These plants are the group of species most susceptible to two fires in short succession. Plants that have seeds stored in the soil usually have some residual seedbank remaining in the soil following post-fire germination. For these species, a second fire before seedlings mature may severely reduce population numbers but it may not eliminate species locally. However, in some places, after some fires, the entire soil seedbank may be exhausted, eg. Restionaceae and Epacridaceae (Meney et al. 1994), *Grevillea* (Auld unpubl.) and local extinction will occur if two fires occur close enough together to kill seedlings from the first fire before they are mature. Ideally, as land managers with concerns for the conservation of biodiversity, we should allow the interval between fires to be long enough not only simply for plant species to mature, but at a minimum, several fruiting seasons beyond this so that a sufficiently large seedbank can be established before the next fire occurs.

### *Fire Intensity*

How hot a fire is will depend on how much combustible fuel is available, how dry this fuel is, the topography of the area and the weather conditions, such as humidity and windspeed. When an area is burnt, the important thing for plants and animals is how much heat is produced, and in many areas around Sydney, this usually varies markedly even on a very small scale (i.e., over tens of meters). How much heat a fire produces can affect the survival of plants. In intense fires there is likely to be higher levels of resprouting plants killed, and longer periods needed before the next fire for recovery, than in mild fires. For plants, the more heat produced by a fire, the greater are the opportunities for seedling recruitment and the greater the magnitude of seedlings that are recruited (Auld & O'Connell 1991). Many plant species have seeds which lie dormant in the soil and for a number of these the amount of soil heating that occurs during the passage of a fire will govern the degree of germination after the fire. This heat response is widespread in many plant families, particularly legumes, in fire-prone communities throughout the world (Martin et al. 1975, Jeffery et al. 1988, Auld & O'Connell 1991, Keeley 1991). Bradstock and Auld (1995) have shown that in Hawkesbury sandstone soil around Sydney, it is the amount of fine fuel that is consumed during a fire that governs the degree of soil heating.

### *Fire season*

Given the prevalence of arson and widespread hazard reduction burning for the protection of life and property, fires can now be expected to occur at just about any time of the year in the Sydney Region. The question is, for the long-term survival of plants does it matter when the vegetation is burnt? In Sydney, Bradstock and Bedward (1992) have suggested that seedling survival after fire is largely independent of season of burn because rainfall is very variable. Although there is a trend for wetter periods in late summer/autumn and drier periods in spring this pattern is not strong enough to allow accurate predictions about the impact of season of burn on seedling survival post-fire. Perhaps the most critical role season of burning may play is in influencing fire intensity. Fires in the hot dry summer months when fuel moisture is low will generally be of higher intensities than burns in winter when the vegetation is moister, an ambient temperatures are lower.

### *Fire Spatial Extent*

What is the impact of the spatial extent of fires on plants? In Sydney, fires come in all shapes and sizes. Some burn very extensive areas, while others may only burn a hectare or so. Within the boundaries of a burnt area, fires may be widespread and burn most of the vegetation or leave large parts of the vegetation unburnt or simply lightly scorched. All fires will be different, depending on the terrain, rate of fire spread, amount of fuel available and its moisture content and weather conditions and natural or man-made fire breaks. This results in a patchiness of fires in area and intensity.

For plants, the spatial extent of fires may be important where burns occur on a very small scale (a few hectares). In such cases, native animals from surrounding unburnt vegetation may graze heavily on the new green shoots that appear after fire and hence, cause a decline in some plant species. These native animals may also consume many of the seeds that are produced in the first few years after fire for those fire-sensitive plants that are trying to replenish their soil seedbanks. This will slow the rate of recovery of such plants.

## Study Species

The threatened species examined, *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* spp. (Proteaceae), are all killed by fire (fire-sensitive, see Gill 1981) and rely on germination from a soil seedbank for persistence at a site after a fire. They are all restricted to the vicinity of Sydney (Figure 1). Threat codes are from Briggs and Leigh (1996).


<<PB>>


166 Auld, T. D. and Scott, J.

*Darwinia biflora* (Cheel) B.Briggs. Vulnerable. A small shrub to 1 m in height in woodland communities mainly in the Hornsby Plateau area in the northern suburbs of Sydney and associated with the Hammondville soil group (Burkitt, Wilson & Benson 1984). The largest populations occur in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, with small outliers in Lane Cove National Park, Marramarra National Park and Pennant Hills Park. This species is threatened by habitat loss, disturbance leading to weed invasion and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia diminuta* B Briggs. Rare. A small shrub to 60 cm in height in woodland and heath communities. Found on sandstone in a few localities in Royal National Park, Heathcote National Park, Garawarra State Recreation Area and Kelly's Falls to the south of Sydney and Garigal National Park in the northern Sydney suburbs. *D. diminuta* is threatened by habitat loss, site disturbance and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia glaucophylla* B. Briggs. Rare. A spreading prostrate shrub in heath. Confined to a few localities on sandstone in the Gosford area north of Sydney. *D. glaucophylla* is threatened by urban development and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia procera* B. Briggs. Rare. An erect shrub to 2 m in height in heath to open forest communities. Mostly confined to sheltered gullies and creek banks on sandstone. Restricted to a few localities between Garigal NP and Brisbane Water NP, in the northern suburbs of Sydney. *D. procera* is threatened by habitat loss, urban runoff and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Grevillea caleyi* R.Br. Endangered. A shrub to 4m by 4m occurring on laterite soils in open forests or low open forests and restricted to roughly a 6 x 6 km area centred on the northern Sydney suburb of Terrey Hills. Habitat destruction has divided the original distribution of the species into a series of discrete population fragments (Scott et al. 1995) separated by urban development (houses, roads, business parks etc). Some 85% of the former habitat of *G. caleyi* has been lost to urban development. Only two of the remaining sites are relatively undisturbed and only one of these two has any long-term protection as it occurs in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park. The remaining large patches are highly disturbed. The major threats to the survival of *G. caleyi* arise from human interference in the environment. These threats range from loss of habitat through clearing, urbanisation and associated infrastructure, changes in landuse and an inappropriate fire regime, to localised disturbance at sites including invasion of weed species and the dumping of rubbish (Scott et al. 1995).

*Grevillea longifolia* R.Br. Rare. A bushy shrub 2-4 m in height by the same wide. It is found in the southern half of the Sydney Region and Woronora plateau and the Jamieson Valley of the Blue Mountains. Usually found in moist areas adjacent to creeks in open forest, but occasionally on escarpments and ridgetops in woodlands on Hawkesbury sandstone. *G. longifolia* is threatened by urban development, runoff, weed encroachment and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Grevillea shiressii* Blakley. Vulnerable. A bushy shrub 2-5 m in height. Found only on the banks of two creeks in closed forest in Brisbane Water National Park in the north of Sydney on soils derived from Narrabeen group geology. *G. shiressii* is threatened by disturbance (a fire trail passes through one population) and an inappropriate fire regime.

## The Effects of the Fire Regime on Threatened Plant Species

For all study species, demographic data were collated on threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species (Scott 1986, Auld et al. 1991, Auld et al. 1993, Auld and Tozer 1995, Scott et al. 1995) and the impacts of components of the fire regime were assessed. A summary of the significant demographic characteristics of our threatened study species is presented in Table 1.

### *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae)

As the *Darwinia* spp. studied are all killed by fire, a fire-free period is needed after any one fire to allow seedlings to mature and replenish the soil seedbank. Plants can produce a few fruits two years after fire. As plants grow, fecundity increases and for all *Darwinia* species, soil seedbanks should increase rapidly 5-10 years after a fire. Most of the annually produced seed-crop is released in a viable, dormant state and would be incorporated into this seedbank, although there is some yearly variation in the proportion of non dormant seeds produced (eg. *D. glaucophylla*, Table 1).

For *D. biflora*, some 75% of the dormant seed released in any one annual seed-crop becomes non dormant and has germinated by 24 months after release, i.e., most seeds from any one seed-crop are short-lived in the soil. The seedbank should buildup in the soil rapidly after a site is burnt, but the seedbank will also decline rapidly should adult plants senesce. The low level of seed longevity in the soil in *D. biflora* (Table 1) suggests that both adult survival and the level of adult fecundity are the critical factors that govern persistence of the soil seedbank. As seeds decay rapidly in the soil, adult plants must regularly produce seeds to maintain a soil seedbank. The longevity of annual seed inputs to the soil seedbank is currently unknown for the other *Darwinia* spp. However, for *D. diminuta*, *D. glaucophylla* and *D. procera* the seedbank size is likely to be much larger than in *D. biflora*, given the higher fecundity levels in these species (Figure 2).

The fate of those seeds in the soil which lose their dormancy and germinate is unknown. It seems likely that

All *Grevillea* species studied were killed by fire and relied on seed germination after a fire to maintain populations. For all species, the magnitude of the soil seedbank will be largely controlled by the levels of adult fecundity, mammal seed predation and adult mortality.

In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia*, seedlings do not flower and produce seeds before 2.5-5 years of age. Fecundity is low in *G. caleyi* with only about 3% of flowers resulting in mature seed (Scott 1986). The level of fecundity in both *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia* increases until around 10 years of age in response to plant growth (Figure 3). No fecundity estimates have been made for *G. shiressii*. In contrast, *G. shiressii* seeds have a lipid body attachment and some 28% of seed are dispersed by ants.
